title: Listen well, handle complaints, and say no with respect

say: Listen well, handle complaints, and say no with respect.
This is the video for module two of Customer Care and Respectful Communication.
Most customer problems start with a misunderstanding: the wrong size, the wrong day, pick-up when she meant delivery. Careful listening prevents many complaints.

panel.heading: Three conversations that test care
items: Turning a complaint into a fair fix

say: When something does go wrong, a complaint is a chance to fix it. Many unhappy customers never complain. They simply stop coming.

panel.heading: Three conversations that test care
items: Turning a complaint into a fair fix

say: And respectful care does not mean saying yes to everything.

panel.heading: Three conversations that test care
items: Turning a complaint into a fair fix

say: For example, Funmi runs a food business in Ibadan. Mrs Adeyemi calls to order for a church women's meeting. Funmi listens fully, with her notebook open.
Open questions invite her to explain. What is the event, and how many people? About 60 women. Is there anything the guests can't eat? About 10 prefer food without pepper.
Funmi paraphrases: so, 60 packs, and 10 of them without pepper. Mrs Adeyemi corrects her: 10 of the 60, not 10 extra. Without that, Funmi might have cooked 70 packs.
Then closed questions pin down the date, time, and delivery or pick-up.
At about 2,500 naira a pack, that is 150,000 naira, with a 50 percent deposit of 75,000. She reads it all back, then sends the summary by WhatsApp so both have it in writing.

panel.heading: Listen, ask, paraphrase, confirm
panel.rule: Repeat every number back, then send a written summary

say: For example, Musa runs a dry-cleaning shop in Kaduna. Mr Bello returns angrily. His white agbada, cleaned for about 4,000 naira, has a yellow stain, and he needs it on Saturday.

panel.heading: Acknowledge, understand, resolve
items: Write the promise, then follow up

say: Acknowledge first. Thank you for bringing it back, Sir. I'm sorry, I can see the stain. Avoid non-apologies like sorry if you feel that way.

panel.heading: Acknowledge, understand, resolve
items: Write the promise, then follow up

say: Understand. Musa checks the drop-off ticket, which says no stains. He does not argue, or blame his staff in front of the customer.

panel.heading: Acknowledge, understand, resolve
items: Write the promise, then follow up

say: Resolve. Option A, a free re-clean by Thursday, with a full refund if the stain remains. Option B, an immediate refund. Mr Bello chooses A.

panel.heading: Acknowledge, understand, resolve
items: Write the promise, then follow up

say: Musa writes the promise on a new ticket, calls when it is ready, and later asks how the wedding went. Mr Bello comes back the next month with three more outfits.

say: A respectful no has three parts. No, said clearly. A short, honest reason. And what you can do instead.

card.title: No, reason, alternative
card.note: Grace keeps the customer and avoids a new debt.

say: Mrs Okon picks goods worth 12,000 naira and asks to pay at month end. Grace says: Aunty, I'm sorry, I can't give credit anymore. When some debts weren't paid, I couldn't restock.

card.title: No, reason, alternative
card.note: Grace keeps the customer and avoids a new debt.

say: Then the alternative. They choose the most urgent items, rice and cooking oil, for the 5,000 she has today.

card.title: No, reason, alternative
card.note: Grace keeps the customer and avoids a new debt.

say: Grace holds the other 7,000 naira of goods, with her name on them, for three days.
Mrs Okon is a little disappointed but not insulted, and keeps shopping with Grace. Say the reason once, kindly, and keep your rules the same for everyone.

say: People tend to match the volume around them, so lower your voice and slow down. Let them finish. Interrupting adds fuel.

panel.heading: When a customer is shouting
items: Lower your voice and slow down
Use their title, name the feeling

say: Use their title and name the feeling: Sir, I can hear you're very frustrated.

panel.heading: When a customer is shouting
items: Lower your voice and slow down

say: Move to a quieter spot if you can, and offer a choice, which gives back a sense of control.

panel.heading: When a customer is shouting
items: Lower your voice and slow down
Use their title, name the feeling

say: Frustration is understandable. Abuse is not. Give one calm warning: I can't continue while you insult me. If it continues, end the conversation and ask a colleague or neighbour to stand with you.

panel.rule: Abuse: one calm warning, then end the conversation

say: If a customer threatens you or becomes physical, move away, call for help, and let the goods or money go. You can report serious threats afterwards.

panel.heading: When to stop and protect yourself

cards.d: Do not argue or try to win. Move to a safe place, call for help, and let goods or money go.
Do not argue or ask them to taste again. Replace or refund, and remove that batch from sale.
Stop replying and, if needed, block and report the number.

say: If someone says food tastes or smells off, apologise, replace or refund it, and remove that batch until you have checked it. Food safety comes before any argument.

say: To remember. Ask open questions first. Paraphrase and confirm every detail. Handle complaints with feelings first, facts second, then two options.
Say no with a reason and an alternative. And put your safety first.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Open questions first, closed ones last
